gradingDesign.rule: All variable student evidence is graded only in the final two BusyBee responses.

questions.prompt: In the fixed Northern Hemisphere setup, fire South to North with direct aim. Which way does the shell deflect relative to the target?
In the fixed Northern Hemisphere setup, fire North to South with direct aim. Which way does the shell deflect relative to the target?
In the fixed Northern Hemisphere setup, fire West to East with direct aim. Which way does the shell deflect relative to the target?
In the fixed Northern Hemisphere setup, fire East to West with direct aim. Which way does the shell deflect relative to the target?
Which statement correctly compares the shell path in an inertial overhead frame with the path seen by an observer rotating with Earth?
What happens to the apparent Coriolis deflection when the launch direction is reversed in the fixed Northern Hemisphere setup?

Compare your direct-aim trials in all four launch directions. Cite the observed miss direction for each trial and explain how reversing north-south or east-west motion changed the apparent deflection.
questions.rubricText:
@[Always] Grading feedback: Grade the four-direction evidence and the relationship between projectile velocity direction and apparent Coriolis deflection.
a. Full credit: Cites accurate outcomes for all four directions and explains that reversing velocity reverses the sideways apparent deflection in the rotating frame. Partial credit: Gives the correct reversal pattern with incomplete trial evidence. No credit: Claims every direction deflects the same way or provides no usable trial results.

questions.prompt: Write a claim-evidence-reasoning conclusion explaining the Coriolis effect. Cite one direct-aim miss and one corrected-aim hit, then explain why the shell can move straight in an inertial frame while appearing curved to the rotating observer.
questions.rubricText:
@[Always] Grading feedback: Grade the frame-based claim, trial evidence, and explanation of the apparent deflection.
a. Full credit: Cites a valid miss and corrected hit, distinguishes the inertial and rotating observations, and explains that the ground, cannon, target, and observer rotate beneath an inertially moving shell. Partial credit: Gives a mostly correct frame explanation with incomplete evidence or weak correction reasoning. No credit: Treats the Coriolis effect as an unexplained physical sideways push or provides no relevant evidence.
